definition: The compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal or by the ammonium ion. Magnesium sulfate, zinc chloride and potassium nitrate are all salts; each acid names its own salt family.
msAccepts: compound formed when acid hydrogen is replaced by a metal/ammonium
acid + base reaction product containing the acid's anion and a metal or ammonium cation
msAvoids: restricting 'salt' to sodium chloride — table salt is one member of a huge family
saying a salt always contains a metal — ammonium salts do not

definition: A salt in which the acid's hydrogen has been replaced by the ammonium ion NH₄⁺ — for example ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl, and ammonium sulfate, (NH₄)₂SO₄. No metal atom is present.
msAccepts: salt containing the NH₄⁺ ion
NH₄Cl and (NH₄)₂SO₄ as examples
msAvoids: writing ammonium as NH₃ — the ion carries four hydrogens and a positive charge
calling ammonium a metal

definition: A substance that neutralises an acid by combining with its hydrogen ions to produce water. In this specification: metal oxides, metal hydroxides and ammonia; in proton-transfer terms, a proton acceptor.
msAccepts: proton acceptor
neutralises acids; metal oxides, hydroxides and ammonia act as bases
msAvoids: listing carbonates among the specification's bases
using 'base' and 'alkali' interchangeably — an alkali is a soluble base

definition: An ionic compound of a metal with the oxide ion O²⁻; a base. Reacts with acids to give a salt and water — copper(II) oxide with hot dilute sulfuric acid gives blue copper(II) sulfate solution.
msAccepts: metal oxide + acid → salt + water
contains the O²⁻ ion which accepts H⁺ to form water
msAvoids: saying metal oxides dissolve in water generally — most are insoluble
forgetting that most oxide–acid reactions need heating

definition: A base that is soluble in water; a solution that is a source of hydroxide (OH⁻) ions. Sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, calcium hydroxide (slightly) and ammonia solution are the alkalis to know.
msAccepts: soluble base
source of hydroxide ions in solution
msAvoids: calling copper(II) oxide an alkali — it is a base that does not dissolve
saying all bases are alkalis

definition: Dissolved ammonia acting as an alkali: NH₃ reacts reversibly with water to form ammonium ions and hydroxide ions, NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, so the solution is weakly alkaline.
msAccepts: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
weak alkali because only some ammonia reacts with water
msAvoids: writing ammonia solution as NH₄OH
omitting the reversible arrow — the reaction is an equilibrium

definition: The reaction between an acid and a base (or alkali) in which hydrogen ions meet hydroxide ions to form water: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). A salt is the other product.
msAccepts: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O as the ionic equation for all acid–alkali neutralisations
acid + base → salt + water
msAvoids: giving the full equation when the ionic equation is asked for
saying neutralisation always needs heating — acid/alkali reactions are instant

definition: An equation showing only the ions that actually take part in a reaction, with spectator ions and unchanged species left out. State symbols are still required for the species shown.
msAccepts: equation with spectator ions omitted
shows only reacting species with state symbols
msAvoids: including spectator ions in the final ionic equation
dropping the state symbols — (aq) and (s) carry marks

definition: An ion present in a reaction mixture that is unchanged by it — it appears identically on both sides of the full equation and is omitted from the ionic equation.
msAccepts: ion not changed by the reaction
same ion on both sides of the full equation; excluded from the ionic equation
msAvoids: calling spectators products or reactants
striking out an ion that changes state or formula

definition: The ranking of metals by reactivity that predicts acid behaviour: metals above hydrogen react with dilute acids to give hydrogen, the higher the more vigorous; metals below hydrogen do not react.
msAccepts: position decides whether a metal reacts with dilute acid
above hydrogen → salt + hydrogen; below → no reaction
msAvoids: mixing sodium or potassium with acid in a described method — far too violent
saying copper reacts slowly with dilute acids

definition: Describes a substance that dissolves in water. Guaranteed soluble: all sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds, and all nitrates — the two rules that anchor every salt-preparation method.
msAccepts: dissolves in water
all Na/K/NH₄ compounds and all nitrates are soluble
msAvoids: saying 'dissolves in anything' — the rules are about water
forgetting that soluble reactants rule out the excess-solid method

definition: Describes a substance that does not (appreciably) dissolve in water. Common carbonates and most hydroxides are insoluble; silver and lead(II) chlorides and barium, calcium and lead(II) sulfates are the key exceptions to otherwise soluble families.
msAccepts: does not dissolve in water (or dissolves only very slightly)
chlorides except Ag/Pb(II); sulfates except Ba/Ca/Pb(II); most carbonates and hydroxides insoluble
msAvoids: claiming absolutely nothing dissolves — 'almost insoluble' substances leave a trace
missing calcium hydroxide's slight solubility

definition: More than enough of a reactant to use the other one up. In salt preparations the insoluble reactant is added in excess; the visible leftover proves all the acid has reacted and is removed by filtration.
msAccepts: added in excess to ensure all the acid reacts
leftover solid shows the acid has been neutralised
msAvoids: adding exactly equal amounts — you cannot judge it and unreacted acid ruins purity
using 'excess' for the acid side in the excess-solid method

definition: Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid by pouring through filter paper. Used twice in salt preparations: to remove excess solid before crystallising, and to collect precipitated or crystallised product.
msAccepts: residue stays on the paper; filtrate passes through
separates insoluble solid from solution
msAvoids: filtering a true solution to remove dissolved salt — solutions pass straight through
confusing residue (wanted solid on the paper) with filtrate

definition: The technique for finding exactly what volumes of two solutions neutralise each other, using an indicator; the same volumes are then mixed again without the indicator to make the salt.
msAccepts: measure reacting volumes with an indicator, then repeat without it
used when both reactants are solutions (Na/K/NH₄ salts)
msAvoids: leaving the indicator in the preparation — it would contaminate the product
using the excess-solid method when both reactants dissolve

definition: The point at which an indicator changes colour during a titration. Close to — but not identical with — exact neutralisation, because the pH swings so steeply that a single drop completes the change.
msAccepts: indicator colour-change point
marks the neutralisation volume to within a drop
msAvoids: equating endpoint with exact neutrality
using universal indicator to find an endpoint — no single sharp change

definition: Indicator that is red in acidic solutions and yellow in alkaline ones; between pH 3.1 and 4.4 it shows a red-yellow mixture (orange), which is the titration endpoint colour when acid is added to alkali.
msAccepts: red in acid, yellow in alkali, orange at the endpoint
usable for titrations involving acid added to alkali
msAvoids: saying it gives a pH value — it sorts acid from alkali
expecting the colour flip exactly at pH 7

definition: Water chemically bound into a salt's crystal lattice as the crystals form, written after a dot in the formula — CuSO₄·5H₂O carries five waters per formula unit.
msAccepts: water chemically bonded into the crystal structure
shown as ·nH₂O in the formula
msAvoids: treating the waters as damp on the outside — they are part of the lattice
copying n between different salts — each salt has its own number

definition: Describes a salt that contains water of crystallisation — the blue crystals of copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO₄·5H₂O, are the chapter's example.
msAccepts: salt containing water of crystallisation
CuSO₄·5H₂O is the hydrated form
msAvoids: spelling it 'hydrous'
confusing hydrated salts with wet crystals — the water is chemically bound

definition: Describes a salt with no water of crystallisation — 'without water'. Evaporating a copper(II) sulfate solution to dryness gives white anhydrous CuSO₄ instead of blue hydrated crystals.
msAccepts: without water of crystallisation
white CuSO₄ is the anhydrous form
msAvoids: using anhydrous to mean simply 'dry on the outside'
heating hydrated crystals to dryness and still calling them the blue hydrated salt

definition: A reaction that produces a precipitate — for salt preparation, mixing two soluble salt solutions so the insoluble salt forms as a solid while the spectator ions stay dissolved.
msAccepts: reaction producing an insoluble solid from two solutions
metal part as nitrate + non-metal part as Na/K salt
msAvoids: calling any gas-producing reaction a precipitation
using an acid plus a carbonate and calling the fizz a precipitate

definition: A solid formed by a chemical reaction involving liquids or gases; in insoluble-salt preparation it appears when two clear solutions are mixed — a fine white, yellow or coloured solid in the liquid.
msAccepts: insoluble solid formed on mixing solutions
name and colour both required — e.g. white precipitate of silver chloride
msAvoids: omitting the colour when asked to describe observations
thinking the solid was dissolved in one of the starting solutions

definition: The acid–base model used at this level: an acid donates a proton (a hydrogen ion, H⁺) and a base accepts one. Reading reactions this way classifies species water cannot classify by its ions alone.
msAccepts: acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor
follow the H⁺: who gives it, who takes it
msAvoids: naming the theories when only the definitions are required
saying a base must contain hydroxide — ammonia accepts protons without any

definition: The H₃O⁺ ion formed when a water molecule accepts a proton from an acid; the ion usually written simply as H⁺(aq). Its formation bond is a dative covalent bond from the oxygen.
msAccepts: H₃O⁺ — water plus a proton
what H⁺(aq) really means in solution
msAvoids: being unable to write H₃O⁺ when H⁺(aq) is accepted too
thinking the name must be memorised — it need not be

definition: A covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from one atom — the O→H bond in H₃O⁺. Also called a co-ordinate bond; once formed it behaves exactly like any other covalent bond.
msAccepts: bond where both electrons in the shared pair come from one atom
O donates its lone pair to H⁺ in H₃O⁺
msAvoids: drawing it with one electron from each atom
treating it as weaker or different once formed

definition: The general acid–base theory defining an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor; unlike the ion-in-water model, it applies beyond aqueous solution.
msAccepts: acid donates a proton, base accepts a proton
applies to reactions outside aqueous solution
msAvoids: believing the theory name itself is examinable — it is not required
confusing the donor/acceptor assignments in a given equation
